title: Atenolol and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Tenormin?
excerpt: Can you drink on atenolol? How alcohol and atenolol lower blood pressure together, why atenolol can hide low blood sugar, why never to skip a dose, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on atenolol? How alcohol and atenolol lower blood pressure together, hide low blood sugar signs, why never to skip a dose, and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most people who take atenolol (brand name Tenormin) can have an occasional drink, and many doctors are fine with light drinking alongside a meal. The trouble is that alcohol and atenolol push in the same direction. Both can lower your blood pressure, and atenolol also stops your heart from speeding up to make up for it. Put them together and some people get dizzy, light-headed, or faint, especially when they stand up quickly or drink more than usual. Atenolol can also hide the early warning signs of low blood sugar, and alcohol makes low blood sugar more likely. That combination matters most for people with diabetes. Over the long run, regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure and can set off heart rhythm problems, which works against the very reason you were prescribed atenolol.

**The quick rules:** Ask your prescriber whether alcohol is OK for you and how much, because the answer depends on why you take atenolol and what else you take. Never skip, delay, or stop a dose so you can drink. Stopping suddenly can cause a dangerous rebound, and the label carries a boxed warning about it. If you do drink, keep it light and slow, eat first, drink water alongside, and stand up slowly. If you have diabetes, check your blood sugar more often and don't rely on a racing heart or shakiness to warn you of a low.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how atenolol and alcohol interact in general terms. It is not a substitute for advice from the doctor or pharmacist who knows your heart, your kidneys, your dose, and your other medicines. **Talk to your doctor before drinking on atenolol if** you take it after a heart attack, for angina, or for a heart rhythm problem, if you also take a water pill (including the combination pill Tenoretic) or other blood pressure medicine, if you have kidney disease, or if you have diabetes. **Get medical help right away (call 911 in the US) if** you faint, have chest pain or pressure, struggle to breathe, have a very slow pulse with dizziness or confusion, or have signs of low blood sugar that don't improve with sugar, such as confusion, slurred speech, or drowsiness that looks like being drunk.

## How Atenolol and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

Atenolol is a **beta blocker**. It blocks the effect of adrenaline on beta-1 receptors, which sit mostly in the heart. That makes your heart beat more slowly and less forcefully, which lowers blood pressure, eases the heart's workload, and helps prevent angina (chest pain from a heart that isn't getting enough oxygen). Doctors call atenolol "cardioselective" because, at usual doses, it mainly targets the heart rather than the lungs and blood vessels. That sets it apart from older, non-selective beta blockers such as propranolol.

Alcohol affects the same system from a few directions at once.

### 1. Both lower blood pressure in the short term

In the first few hours after drinking, alcohol tends to relax and widen blood vessels. For many people that means blood pressure dips for a while. Normally your body responds to a dip by speeding up your heart to keep blood flowing to your brain. Atenolol blunts exactly that response. So the drop that a healthy person barely notices can feel like dizziness, a "head rush" when you stand, or weakness in someone on a beta blocker.

This effect is usually mild with one drink. It gets more likely when you drink several drinks, drink quickly, drink on an empty stomach, are dehydrated, are in a hot room or hot tub, or also take other blood pressure medicines.

### 2. Regular heavy drinking pushes blood pressure up

Over days and weeks, the picture flips. Drinking heavily on a regular basis is one of the best-known lifestyle causes of high blood pressure, and blood pressure often climbs during the hours after a heavy session wears off. That works directly against atenolol. People who drink heavily may find their blood pressure harder to control even when they take every dose. Our guide to [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) explains this two-phase pattern in more detail.

### 3. Alcohol can trigger heart rhythm trouble

Heavy drinking, and especially binge drinking, can set off atrial fibrillation and other irregular rhythms. Doctors sometimes call this "holiday heart." Atenolol is often prescribed to help control heart rate in conditions like these, so a night of heavy drinking can undo some of what it's doing. If you notice your heart racing or fluttering after drinking, our article on a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers what's going on and when to worry.

### 4. Low blood sugar, with the alarm turned down

This is the part of the interaction people most often miss, and it's covered in its own section below. In short: alcohol can lower blood sugar, and atenolol can mute some of the symptoms that warn you it's happening.

### What doesn't happen: alcohol and atenolol levels

Some medicines interact with alcohol because they're both processed by the same liver enzymes, which can change how much drug ends up in your blood. Atenolol is different. It's water-soluble and is cleared mainly by the kidneys, largely unchanged, rather than broken down by the liver. So alcohol isn't expected to raise or lower atenolol levels in the way it can for some liver-processed drugs. The interaction is about **effects adding up**, not one drug changing the level of the other.

That kidney route does have one practical consequence. Heavy drinking can lead to vomiting, poor fluid intake, and dehydration, and dehydration can temporarily reduce how well your kidneys work. Atenolol doses are already lowered for people with reduced kidney function for this reason. If you're ever badly dehydrated or unable to keep fluids down, especially if you have kidney disease, that's a reason to call your doctor rather than just wait it out.

## Atenolol, Alcohol, and Low Blood Sugar

Your liver keeps your blood sugar steady between meals partly by making new glucose. While it's busy processing alcohol, it does less of that. In someone who has eaten, this usually doesn't matter much. But if you drink without eating, drink heavily, or take diabetes medicines that lower blood sugar (such as insulin or sulfonylureas like glipizide or glyburide), alcohol can cause a real low, sometimes hours after you stop drinking, including overnight.

Normally your body sounds the alarm when blood sugar drops. Adrenaline kicks in and you feel your heart pounding, your hands shaking, and a sense of nervousness. Beta blockers like atenolol can blunt the fast heartbeat and tremor. The atenolol label warns about this: it says beta blockers may mask the rapid heartbeat that comes with low blood sugar, though other signs such as dizziness and sweating may still show up.

Put those together and you can end up with a low that's both more likely and harder to notice. To make it worse, the confusion, clumsiness, and slurred speech of low blood sugar look a lot like being drunk, so the people around you may not realize anything is wrong.

Because atenolol is cardioselective, it's thought to interfere less with blood sugar recovery than non-selective beta blockers like propranolol. It still blunts the warning signs, though, so the precautions apply.

**If you have diabetes and take atenolol:**

- Talk to your diabetes care team before drinking. They can tell you whether to adjust anything on days you drink.
- Eat a meal with carbohydrates before or while drinking, and don't drink on an empty stomach.
- Check your blood sugar more often when drinking, before bed, and again the next morning. A continuous glucose monitor with low alerts helps if you have one.
- Pay attention to **sweating**, which usually isn't masked by beta blockers, and to unexplained confusion or drowsiness.
- Keep fast-acting sugar on hand, and make sure someone you're with knows you have diabetes and what a low looks like.
- Wear or carry medical identification.

For a broader look at drinking with diabetes, see our [alcohol and blood sugar guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025), and our article on [low blood sugar after drinking](/never-hungover/low-blood-sugar-after-drinking) for the symptoms to watch for.

## What the Label and Official Guidance Say

The atenolol prescribing information doesn't set a specific alcohol limit. What it does carry are the warnings that shape how drinking fits around it:

- **A boxed warning about stopping suddenly.** The label warns that people with coronary artery disease who stop atenolol abruptly can have severe worsening of angina, and that heart attacks and dangerous heart rhythms have been reported. It advises tapering under a doctor's supervision when atenolol needs to stop. This is the most important reason never to skip doses for a night out.
- **A warning about masked low blood sugar** in people with diabetes, as described above.
- **Cautions about combining with other drugs that lower blood pressure or heart rate**, which is relevant because alcohol behaves like one more blood-pressure-lowering factor in the short term.
- **Dose adjustment for kidney function**, since atenolol is cleared by the kidneys.

Most drug-interaction references list alcohol and beta blockers as a moderate interaction, mainly because of the added blood-pressure-lowering effect. In plain terms, that means it's not an absolute "never," but it is something to plan around and discuss with your prescriber.

General public health guidance on alcohol also applies. US dietary guidance suggests that adults who drink limit themselves to two drinks or fewer a day for men and one or fewer for women, and notes that drinking less is better for health than drinking more. Your prescriber may set a lower limit for you, or advise against drinking at all, depending on your heart condition. Their advice comes first. If you're not sure how much alcohol is in what you're drinking, our guide to [alcohol content by drink](/never-hungover/alcohol-content-by-drink) helps you count standard drinks accurately.

## Why You Should Never Skip a Dose to Drink

It's a common instinct: "I'm going out tonight, so I'll skip my pill to be safe." With atenolol, that instinct is backwards.

When you take a beta blocker every day, your body adjusts to having those receptors blocked. If the drug suddenly disappears, the heart can become extra sensitive to adrenaline for a while. That can mean a fast heart rate, a jump in blood pressure, and, for people with heart disease, worse chest pain or a heart attack. Alcohol can add to this by raising heart rate and blood pressure as it wears off. Skipping a dose and then drinking heavily stacks two risks on top of each other.

If you're worried about combining your dose with alcohol, the safer options are to drink less, not drink that day, or ask your prescriber or pharmacist ahead of time. Don't change the timing or amount of your dose on your own.

## Atenolol vs. Metoprolol vs. Propranolol: Does It Matter Which Beta Blocker?

All beta blockers share the core interaction: alcohol plus a beta blocker can lower blood pressure more than either alone, and the drug can blunt the low-blood-sugar warning signs. But they differ in ways that matter a little for drinking.

| | Atenolol | Metoprolol | Propranolol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main target | Heart (cardioselective) | Heart (cardioselective) | Heart, lungs, and blood vessels (non-selective) |
| How it's cleared | Mostly by the kidneys | Mostly by the liver | Mostly by the liver |
| Reaches the brain | Less (water-soluble) | More (fat-soluble) | More (fat-soluble) |
| Usual dosing | Once or twice daily | Twice daily (tartrate) or once daily (succinate ER) | Two to four times daily, or once daily (ER) |

A few practical points follow from this:

- **Kidneys, not liver.** Because atenolol doesn't depend on the liver, alcohol-related liver changes are less of a concern for its levels. Kidney function matters more.
- **Fewer brain-related side effects.** Atenolol is water-soluble and crosses into the brain less than metoprolol or propranolol. Some people find it causes fewer vivid dreams or sleep problems. That said, alcohol plus any beta blocker can still leave you more tired or sluggish than alcohol alone.
- **Cardioselective, but not perfectly.** At higher doses, atenolol's selectivity fades, so it can still affect the lungs in people with asthma. Drinking doesn't change that, but it's worth knowing if you have breathing problems.

For the side-by-side details, see our guides on [metoprolol and alcohol](/never-hungover/metoprolol-and-alcohol) and [propranolol and alcohol](/never-hungover/propranolol-and-alcohol), or the overview of [beta blockers and alcohol](/never-hungover/beta-blockers-and-alcohol) that covers the whole drug class. If you take atenolol alongside a different kind of blood pressure drug, our [blood pressure medication and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/blood-pressure-medication-and-alcohol) compares how each class interacts with drinking.

## Tenoretic: Atenolol Plus a Water Pill

Atenolol also comes in a combination pill called **Tenoretic**, which adds chlorthalidone, a diuretic (water pill). If that's what you take, the alcohol picture shifts a little:

- Diuretics make you pass more fluid, and alcohol does too. Together they make dehydration more likely, which can deepen the blood pressure drop and the dizziness. See our article on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) for how this works.
- Chlorthalidone can lower potassium and sodium, and heavy drinking with vomiting can push those levels further off.
- Dizziness on standing tends to be more noticeable with two blood-pressure-lowering drugs plus alcohol.

If you take Tenoretic or any other combination of blood pressure medicines, it's worth asking your prescriber specifically about alcohol, rather than relying on general rules.

## Practical Tips If Your Prescriber Says Light Drinking Is OK

If your doctor has said an occasional drink is fine for you, these habits help keep the combination comfortable and safe:

1. **Keep taking atenolol exactly as prescribed.** Same dose, same time.
2. **Start small, especially at first.** The first few times you drink after starting atenolol or changing your dose, have less than usual and see how you feel.
3. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows alcohol absorption and helps protect against low blood sugar.
4. **Alternate with water.** Staying hydrated helps your blood pressure and your kidneys.
5. **Stand up slowly.** Sit on the edge of the bed or chair for a moment before getting up, especially at night.
6. **Skip hot tubs and saunas after drinking.** Heat widens blood vessels too, and stacking that on top of alcohol and atenolol makes fainting more likely.
7. **Don't use alcohol to push through exercise.** Atenolol caps how high your heart rate goes, and alcohol plus exertion plus heat is a poor mix.
8. **Count your drinks honestly.** A large pour of wine or a strong craft beer can be two standard drinks or more.

## Hangover Remedies to Check First on Atenolol

The morning after is when people reach for other medicines, and a few common ones interact with blood pressure treatment:

- **Ibuprofen, naproxen, and other NSAIDs** can raise blood pressure and weaken the effect of blood pressure medicines, including beta blockers, when used regularly. They're also hard on a stomach that alcohol has already irritated. See our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol).
- **Decongestants** like pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) and many "cold and sinus" combinations can raise blood pressure and heart rate. Our page on [Sudafed and alcohol](/never-hungover/sudafed-and-alcohol) covers this.
- **Energy drinks and lots of caffeine** can raise heart rate and blood pressure and may set off palpitations, especially after a night of drinking.
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** doesn't affect blood pressure the way NSAIDs do, but it has its own alcohol rules for the liver. See our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

A pharmacist can quickly check any over-the-counter product against your medicine list. That's a free, five-minute conversation that's worth having.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Mild dizziness when you stand up, which goes away when you sit, is the most common effect of drinking on atenolol. Sit or lie down, drink water, and mention it to your doctor if it keeps happening.

**Call 911 (in the US) or get emergency care if you or someone with you has:**

- Fainting or nearly fainting, especially with a fall or head injury
- Chest pain, pressure, or tightness
- Trouble breathing or wheezing
- A very slow pulse with dizziness, confusion, or extreme tiredness
- A racing, pounding, or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle
- Signs of low blood sugar that don't improve after taking sugar, or someone who can't safely swallow, is very drowsy, or is having a seizure
- Signs of a stroke, such as face drooping, arm weakness, or slurred speech that isn't explained by drinking

If someone on atenolol seems "too drunk" for how much they've had, especially if they have diabetes, consider low blood sugar and check it if you can.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Some people should talk to their prescriber specifically about alcohol before drinking on atenolol, rather than relying on general advice:

- People who take atenolol **after a heart attack, for angina, or for coronary artery disease**
- People with **heart rhythm problems** such as atrial fibrillation
- People with **diabetes**, especially those on insulin or sulfonylureas
- People with **kidney disease**, since atenolol is cleared by the kidneys
- People taking **more than one blood pressure medicine**, including Tenoretic or a separate water pill
- **Older adults**, who are more prone to dizziness and falls
- People who are **pregnant or breastfeeding**, for whom both alcohol and medicine choices need a doctor's input
- Anyone who finds it hard to keep drinking light. A prescriber can help with an honest plan, and there's no judgment in asking.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

If you're reading about atenolol and alcohol because you get rough hangovers, the most effective steps are the plain ones: drink less, drink slower, eat, and hydrate. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also try **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising, not proven. Importantly, **DHM doesn't change how atenolol and alcohol affect your blood pressure, heart rate, or blood sugar**, and there isn't good human research on DHM combined with beta blockers. Ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement to a heart medicine. If they're comfortable with it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) and [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) cover the details.

## The Bottom Line

Atenolol and alcohol interact mainly by adding up their effects. Both lower blood pressure in the short term, and atenolol stops your heart from speeding up to compensate, which is why some people feel dizzy or faint. Atenolol can also hide the racing heart and shakiness that warn of low blood sugar, which matters most if you have diabetes. Over the long term, heavy drinking raises blood pressure and can trigger rhythm problems, working against your treatment. Because atenolol is cleared by the kidneys rather than the liver, alcohol isn't expected to change its levels, but dehydration from heavy drinking still matters.

Keep taking atenolol as prescribed, never skip a dose to drink, and get your alcohol limit from your prescriber rather than from a general rule.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking atenolol?**

Many people on atenolol can have an occasional drink, and many doctors are fine with light drinking alongside a meal. The issue is that alcohol and atenolol both lower blood pressure, and atenolol also stops your heart from speeding up to compensate, so some people feel dizzy or faint. Whether drinking is right for you, and how much, is a question for your prescriber, especially if you take atenolol after a heart attack, for angina, or with other blood pressure medicines.

**Does alcohol change how atenolol works?**

Atenolol is cleared mainly by the kidneys rather than broken down by the liver, so alcohol isn't expected to change atenolol's blood levels in the way it can for some liver-processed drugs. The interaction is mostly about effects adding up: both lower blood pressure. Over time, regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure and can trigger heart rhythm problems, which works against the reason you take atenolol.

**Should I skip my atenolol dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Don't skip, delay, or stop atenolol to make room for drinks unless your prescriber tells you to. The atenolol label carries a boxed warning that stopping suddenly can worsen angina and, in some people, lead to heart attack or dangerous heart rhythms. If you're worried about combining your dose with alcohol, the safer move is to drink less or not at all that day, and ask your doctor or pharmacist how to plan around it.

**Does atenolol hide the signs of low blood sugar?**

It can. Atenolol can blunt the fast heartbeat and shakiness that normally warn you that your blood sugar is dropping. Sweating usually still happens. Alcohol makes low blood sugar more likely, especially if you drink without eating or take insulin or a sulfonylurea. If you have diabetes, check your blood sugar more often when drinking, eat while you drink, and ask your care team for a plan.

**Why do I feel dizzy when I drink on atenolol?**

Alcohol widens blood vessels and can lower blood pressure for a few hours after drinking. Atenolol also lowers blood pressure and keeps your heart rate from rising to make up for it. Together they can cause light-headedness, especially when you stand up quickly, are dehydrated, or drink on an empty stomach. Sit or lie down if it happens, and tell your doctor if it happens often. Fainting, chest pain, or a very slow pulse with confusion needs urgent care.

**How long after taking atenolol can I drink?**

There's no official waiting period. Atenolol is usually taken once or twice a day and works around the clock, so there's no time of day when it's fully out of your system. Rather than timing drinks around doses, keep your dose on schedule, keep any drinking light and slow, eat first, and drink water alongside. Your prescriber can tell you whether any amount of alcohol is reasonable for your situation.

**Can I take ibuprofen or a decongestant for a hangover while on atenolol?**

Check with a pharmacist first. NSAIDs like ibuprofen and naproxen can raise blood pressure and weaken the effect of blood pressure medicines, and they're also hard on the stomach after drinking. Decongestants such as pseudoephedrine can raise blood pressure and heart rate. A pharmacist can suggest an option that fits your medicines and health conditions.

**Is DHM safe to take with atenolol?**

There isn't good human research on DHM combined with atenolol, so it's best to ask your doctor or pharmacist before adding it. DHM is a plant compound studied mostly in animals and lab settings for its effects on alcohol metabolism. It does not change how atenolol and alcohol affect your blood pressure, and it isn't a reason to drink more.
